questions.question: Describe the difference between the Hamiltonian and the Eulerian cycle in graph theory. Use an example graph for each concept. [4 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start (it need not use every edge).
Eulerian cycle: a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start (vertices may be visited several times). An undirected connected graph has one if and only if every vertex has even degree.
So the difference is vertices versus edges: Hamiltonian = each vertex once, Eulerian = each edge once. (The TSP looks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle.)
Example 1 (Hamiltonian, not Eulerian): square 1–2–5–4–1 with a centre vertex 3 joined to 1, 2, 4, 5. The cycle 1–2–3–5–4–1 visits every vertex once. It is not Eulerian: vertices 1, 2, 4, 5 have odd degree 3.
Example 2 (Eulerian, not Hamiltonian): a "bow-tie", two triangles 1–3–4 and 2–3–5 sharing vertex 3. The closed walk 1–3–2–5–3–4–1 uses all 6 edges once (degrees 2, 2, 4, 2, 2 are all even). It is not Hamiltonian: any cycle through all vertices must pass through 3 twice.

rubric.point: Hamiltonian cycle: visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start
Eulerian cycle: uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start
Example graph with a Hamiltonian cycle shown
Example graph with an Eulerian cycle shown

questions.question: Consider the max-flow problem of a directed network with a source node $s$ and the sink node $t$. Let $x_{ij}$ denote the amount of flow between the node $i$ and node $j$. Write the node balanced equation of a node $i$ where $i \ne s$ and $i \ne t$. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
For an intermediate node $i$ the flow out equals the flow in:
$$\sum_{j} x_{ij} - \sum_{j} x_{ji} = 0, \qquad i \ne s,\ i \ne t,$$
where $x_{ij}$ is the flow on arc $(i,j)$ (leaving $i$) and $x_{ji}$ the flow on arc $(j,i)$ (entering $i$), with $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$. (At the source the difference is $+F$ and at the sink $-F$, the flow value.)

rubric.point: Outflow $\sum_j x_{ij}$ minus inflow $\sum_j x_{ji}$
…equals 0 for every intermediate node

questions.question: Define the following concepts in the Ford Fulkerson algorithm for max-flow problem: (i) The Augmenting Path; (ii) the Residual Network corresponding to a feasible flow of amount $x$. [1½ + 1½ + 4 + 1 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) An augmenting path $P$ is a simple directed path from the source $s$ to the sink $t$ in the residual network $G_x$, i.e. every arc on it still has positive residual capacity $r_{ij} > 0$. Its capacity is the bottleneck
$$\delta(P) = \min_{(i,j) \in P} r_{ij},$$
and the flow from $s$ to $t$ can be increased by $\delta(P)$ by sending that much along every arc of $P$ (then $r_{ij} \leftarrow r_{ij} - \delta(P)$, $r_{ji} \leftarrow r_{ji} + \delta(P)$). Ford–Fulkerson stops when no augmenting path exists; the flow is then maximum.
(ii) Given a feasible flow $x$ with capacities $u_{ij}$, the residual network $G_x = (V, E_x)$ has the same nodes, and each arc $(i,j)$ of the network is replaced by two arcs:
• forward arc $(i,j)$ with residual capacity $r_{ij} = u_{ij} - x_{ij}$ (how much more flow can still be sent from $i$ to $j$);
• backward arc $(j,i)$ with residual capacity $r_{ji} = x_{ij}$ (how much of the existing flow can be cancelled by sending it back).
$E_x$ keeps only the arcs with $r_{ij} > 0$. So the residual network shows where extra flow can still be pushed (or undone), and augmenting paths are searched for in it.

rubric.point: Augmenting path: a directed $s$–$t$ path in the residual network (all residual capacities positive)
Its capacity is the bottleneck $\delta(P) = \min r_{ij}$, added to the flow
Residual network: forward residual $r_{ij} = u_{ij} - x_{ij}$
Backward residual $r_{ji} = x_{ij}$; only arcs with positive residual capacity kept

questions.question:
(c) (i) Define the following concepts in the Ford Fulkerson algorithm for max-flow problem: (i) The Augmenting Path; (ii) the Residual Network corresponding to a feasible flow of amount $x$. (iii) Use these concepts to find the maximum flow of the network in Fig. 1:
[1½ + 1½ + 4 + 1 Marks ]
questions.solution:
Start with zero flow: every residual capacity equals the capacity.
1. Augmenting path $P_1$: $s \to 1 \to t$, $\delta(P_1) = \min\{10, 8\} = 8$. Update: $r_{s1} = 2$, $r_{1s} = 8$; $r_{1t} = 0$, $r_{t1} = 8$. Flow = 8.
2. $P_2$: $s \to 2 \to t$, $\delta(P_2) = \min\{6, 10\} = 6$. Update: $r_{s2} = 0$, $r_{2s} = 6$; $r_{2t} = 4$, $r_{t2} = 6$. Flow = 14.
3. $P_3$: $s \to 1 \to 2 \to t$, $\delta(P_3) = \min\{2, 1, 4\} = 1$. Update: $r_{s1} = 1$, $r_{12} = 0$, $r_{2t} = 3$ (and the reverse arcs grow by 1). Flow = 15.
Residual network now: from $s$ only $s \to 1$ ($r = 1$) is open; from 1 both $1 \to 2$ and $1 \to t$ are saturated ($r = 0$). So $t$ cannot be reached: no augmenting path is left and the flow is maximum.
$$\text{max flow} = \delta(P_1) + \delta(P_2) + \delta(P_3) = 8 + 6 + 1 = 15.$$
Final flows: $x_{s1} = 9$, $x_{s2} = 6$, $x_{12} = 1$, $x_{1t} = 8$, $x_{2t} = 7$ (out of $s$: $9 + 6 = 15$; into $t$: $8 + 7 = 15$).

answerImage.alt: Final flow/capacity on each arc: s→1 9/10, s→2 6/6, 1→2 1/1, 1→t 8/8, 2→t 7/10. The saturated arcs s→2, 1→2 and 1→t cross a dashed cut line between A = {s, 1} and B = {2, t}; max flow 15 = cap(A, B) = 6 + 1 + 8.

questions.question:
(c) (i) Define the following concepts in the Ford Fulkerson algorithm for max-flow problem: (i) The Augmenting Path; (ii) the Residual Network corresponding to a feasible flow of amount $x$. (iii) Use these concepts to find the maximum flow of the network in Fig. 1:
(iv) Find the minimum $s$-$t$ cut $(A, B)$ of the max-flow solution for the above network. [1½ + 1½ + 4 + 1 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
After the maximum flow (15) the residual network lets $s$ reach only node 1 ($r_{s1} = 1$; $r_{s2} = 0$, $r_{12} = 0$, $r_{1t} = 0$). The nodes reachable from $s$ form $A$:
$$A = \{s, 1\}, \qquad B = \{2, t\}.$$
Arcs from $A$ to $B$: $s \to 2$ (6), $1 \to 2$ (1), $1 \to t$ (8), so $\text{cap}(A, B) = 6 + 1 + 8 = 15$, which equals the maximum flow (max-flow = min-cut), confirming both. (For comparison: $\{s\}$ gives 16 and $\{s, 1, 2\}$ gives 18.)

rubric.point: $A = \{s, 1\}$, $B = \{2, t\}$ with capacity 15 = max flow

questions.question: Find the minimum spanning tree (MST) of the undirected graph below in Fig. 2, where the distance or cost of various edges are $c_{12} = c_{13} = c_{24} = c_{34} = 1$, $c_{14} = 2$ and $c_{23} = 3$ [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
MST by inspection: there are 4 vertices, so the tree needs $4 - 1 = 3$ edges. The four edges of cost 1 form the cycle 1–2–4–3–1; any three of them connect all four vertices without a cycle. Take
$$T = \{(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)\}, \qquad \text{cost} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.$$
It is minimum because every spanning tree has 3 edges and every edge costs at least 1, so no tree can cost less than 3. The diagonals $(1,4)$ (cost 2) and $(2,3)$ (cost 3) are not used. (Kruskal gives the same: take the unit edges in turn and skip the one that would close the cycle.) Any other choice of three unit edges is an equally good MST.

rubric.point: Three edges of cost 1 chosen that connect all 4 vertices without a cycle
Total cost 3, with a reason it is minimal (diagonals not used)

questions.question: Define mathematically the sub-tour elimination constraints for asymmetric traveling salesman problem (TSP). [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
ATSP subtour elimination constraints ($x_{ij} = 1$ if the salesman goes directly from city $i$ to city $j$):
$$\sum_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S,\ j \ne i} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1, \qquad \forall S \subset V,\ 2 \le |S| \le n - 2.$$
For any proper subset $S$ of cities, the arcs used inside $S$ must be fewer than $|S|$, so they cannot close a cycle on $S$ alone.
Here $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is the set of cities. Without these constraints the assignment constraints ($\sum_i x_{ij} = 1$, $\sum_j x_{ij} = 1$) can be satisfied by several disjoint directed cycles (sub-tours), e.g. $1 \to 2 \to 1$ and $3 \to 4 \to \dots \to n \to 3$; for $S = \{1, 2\}$ that solution has $x_{12} + x_{21} = 2 > 1$ and is cut off.

rubric.point: Variables: $x_{ij} = 1$ if the tour goes directly from $i$ to $j$
$\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S, j \ne i} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1$
For all $S \subset V$ with $2 \le |S| \le n - 2$

questions.question: Define an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm of a minimization problem. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $P$ be a minimisation problem with set of instances $\mathcal{I}$, and let $A$ be an algorithm that returns a feasible solution $A(I)$ for every instance $I \in \mathcal{I}$. $A$ is an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm ($\alpha \ge 1$) if it finds that feasible solution in polynomial time for every instance and
$$A(I) \le \alpha \cdot OPT(I) \quad \text{for all } I \in \mathcal{I},$$
where $OPT(I)$ is the optimal (minimum) value of instance $I$. So the answer is never worse than $\alpha$ times the optimum; the closer $\alpha$ is to 1, the better the guarantee.

rubric.point: Minimisation problem with instances; $A$ returns a feasible solution $A(I)$ for every instance
Runs in polynomial time
$A(I) \le \alpha\, OPT(I)$ for all $I$, with $\alpha \ge 1$

questions.question: Consider the 7 city symmetric TSP with a feasible tour $x = (1, 3, 2, 6, 7, 4, 5)$ where the 1st city is the starting city. Construct a single 2-Opt neighbor of $x$. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
2-opt move: delete two non-adjacent edges $(c_i, c_{i+1})$ and $(c_j, c_{j+1})$ of the tour and reconnect with $(c_i, c_j)$ and $(c_{i+1}, c_{j+1})$; this reverses the cities in positions $i+1, \dots, j$. Positions (not city labels) of $x$: $c_1 = 1, c_2 = 3, c_3 = 2, c_4 = 6, c_5 = 7, c_6 = 4, c_7 = 5$ (city 1 stays first).
Take $i = 2$, $j = 4$: remove the edges $(c_2, c_3) = (3, 2)$ and $(c_4, c_5) = (6, 7)$, add $(3, 6)$ and $(2, 7)$, and reverse the segment in positions 3–4 ("2, 6"):
$$x' = (1, 3, 6, 2, 7, 4, 5).$$
Any other valid choice is also correct, e.g. $i = 1, j = 3$: $(1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 4, 5)$.

rubric.point: Two non-adjacent edges of the tour removed (named)
The two reconnecting edges added (segment reversed)
A valid neighbour tour with city 1 first

questions.question: Write down the mathematical model of the set covering problem. Describe the physical meaning of the constraint sets in the mathematical model. [3½ Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Set $S = \{1, \dots, n\}$ of items and subsets $S_1, \dots, S_m$ of $S$; choosing $S_j$ costs $c_j > 0$; pick subsets that cover every item at minimum cost.
Data: $a_{ij} = 1$ if item $i$ is in $S_j$, $a_{ij} = 0$ otherwise ($i = 1, \dots, n$; $j = 1, \dots, m$).
Decision variables: $x_j = 1$ if subset $S_j$ is chosen, $x_j = 0$ otherwise.
$$\min \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j x_j$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{m} a_{ij} x_j \ge 1, \quad i = 1, \dots, n$$
$$x_j \in \{0, 1\}, \quad j = 1, \dots, m$$
Meaning: the objective is the total cost of the chosen subsets (minimise it). The constraint for item $i$ says that at least one chosen subset contains item $i$, i.e. every item of $S$ is covered at least once. $x_j \in \{0, 1\}$: each subset is either taken or not (no fractions of a subset).

rubric.point: Defines $x_j$ and $a_{ij}$
Objective $\min \sum_j c_j x_j$
Constraints $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \ge 1$ for every item, $x_j \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning: every item is covered by at least one chosen subset

questions.question: A constraint of the mathematical model of the facility location problem is given by $\sum_{i=1}^{m} x_{ij} = 1$, $\forall j$, where $i$ represents the warehouses and $j$ is a customer; $x_{ij}$ is the variable representing whether customer $j$ is served by the warehouse $i$. Described the meaning of this constraint. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer: For each customer $j$, the sum over all $m$ warehouses of the binary $x_{ij}$ is exactly 1. So every customer $j$ is served, and by exactly one warehouse: it cannot be left unserved or split between warehouses (single-source facility location).

rubric.point: Every customer must be served
…by exactly one warehouse

questions.question: Write down the mathematical model of the linear knapsack problem. Describe the physical meaning of the main constraint in the mathematical model. [3½ Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Items $i = 1, \dots, n$, item $i$ has weight $w_i \ge 0$ and value $v_i \ge 0$; the knapsack holds total weight at most $W$. Variables: $x_i = 1$ if item $i$ is put in the knapsack, 0 otherwise.
$$\max \sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i x_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i \le W, \qquad x_i \in \{0, 1\}.$$
(It is assumed that $\sum_i w_i > W$, otherwise everything fits.)
Meaning of the main constraint $\sum_i w_i x_i \le W$: the total weight (or cost) of the items chosen cannot exceed the capacity (budget) of the knapsack.

rubric.point: Binary variables $x_i$ with their meaning
Objective $\max \sum_i v_i x_i$
Capacity constraint $\sum_i w_i x_i \le W$ and $x_i \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning: total weight of chosen items at most the capacity
